messages.subject: stratification vs post-stratification vs multiple covariates
messages.subject_clean: stratification vs post-stratification vs multiple covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am new to using distance sampling and I am confused as to the best way to=
 proceed with my data analysis. The more I read, the less clear things beco=
me so I thought I could request some feedback.

I am trying to determine density estimates for a variety of east African sa=
vannah animals based on data collected over the past year. There are reside=
nt species and migratory species. Density for migratory species should vary=
 by season (wet vs dry) while the density of resident species should remain=
 the same. However, detectability varies between the wet and dry season for=
 all species. Addtionally, cluster size for some species could also influen=
ce detectability.

I thought it would be best to run separate analyses based on season for the=
 migratory species, since detectability and density would vary, but I'm won=
dering if I can somehow stratify the data to return separate detection func=
tions and densities based on seasons. I would still need to account for the=
 changes in detectability based on cluster size though. For the resident sp=
ecies, I'm struggling to understand how to incorporate changes in seasonal =
detectability plus clusters into an analysis - stratification, post-stratif=
ication, or multiple covariates - to return a single density estimate. I ha=
ve run analyses using all three for one species and for the most part, I ge=
t generally the same density estimate. However, I have no idea which method=
 is the most appropriate. I would certainly appreciate any insight. Feel fr=
ee to email me directly at cm...@duke.edu<mailto:cm...@duke.edu> or christy.i=
h...@duke.edu<mailto:christ...@duke.edu>.

Thank you for tolerating what is probably a repetitive email for this lists=
erve!

Christy M. Ihlo
Master of Environmental Management Candidate
Concentration in Ecosystem Science and Conservation
Nicholas School of the Environment, Duke University
christ...@duke.edu
404.313.7786

messages.subject: Power Analysis - R code
messages.body_plain:
I am working on a power analysis for detecting a change between two abund=
ance estimates using a z-test

z =3D (N1-N2)/sgrt(var(N1-N2))

I have wrote the following R code to estimate power:

ZPOWER.2sided =3D function(change,N1,CV,alpha){
  N2=3DN1+(N1*change)
  SD1=3DN1*CV
  SD2=3DN2*CV
  VAR=3D(SD1^2)+(SD2^2)
  qL=3Dqnorm(alpha/2)
  qU=3Dqnorm(1-(alpha/2))
  Z =3D(N1-N2)/sqrt(VAR)
  power =3D (pnorm(qL-Z))+(1-pnorm(qU-Z))
  cbind(N1,N2,change,CV,SD1,SD2,VAR,qL,qU,Z,alpha,power)}
# Where N1 and N2 are the two abundances, change is the desired percent c=
hange, and CV is coefficient of var.

# Example use of function.
ZPOWER.2sided(change=3D-0.2,N1=3D300,CV=3D0.15,alpha=3D0.05)

After writing this code, I found the following code posted at http://www.=
creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/software.html <http://creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/software.html>.

#--------------------------------------------
#Power to detect a change between two time
# points using a z-test.  Not used in book
# chapter
#--------------------------------------------
#alpha level (type I error)
alpha<-0.05=20
#vector of coefficients of var
cvs <- seq(0.05,0.5,by=3D0.05)=20
#vector of true differences
fs <- seq(0,1,by=3D0.1)
lcvs<-length(cvs)
lfs<-length(fs)
res<-matrix(0,lcvs,lfs)
q1<-qnorm(1-(alpha/2))
q2<-qnorm(alpha/2)
s2<-sqrt(2)
#work out power at each level of CV and true diff
for(i1 in 1:lcvs) {
  cv<-cvs[i1]
  for (i2 in 1:lfs) {
    f<-fs[i2]
    z<-f/(s2*cv)
    power =3D (1-pnorm(q1-z)) + pnorm(q2 - z)
    res[i1,i2]<-power
  }
}
#output as a perspective plot
persp(cvs,fs,res)
#--------------------------------------------

A major difference between my code and this code is z=3D(N1-N2)/sqrt(VAR)=
 vs. z=3Df/(s2*cv).

Can someone help me understand the use of sqrt(2)*CV in the denomiator in=
stead of sqrt(VAR)?

Thanks,

Matt

messages.subject: Distance from "the line", or where you happen to be at the time?
messages.subject_clean: Distance from "the line", or where you happen to be at the time?
messages.body_plain:
G'day Distance samplers,

On line transects, is the perpendicular distance to an animal taken from =
the predetermined "line", or from where you happen to be at the time of s=
ighting??  I've had conflicting statistical advice on this.

(We spotlight for ground-dwelling marsupials on islands.  Our transect li=
nes are marked out by reflective tape, but we only walk them once a year,=
 so some of the markers inevitably fall down and we walk "the line" by GP=
S until we can see the next reflector post to aim for.  This, together wi=
th patches of bush that we have to go around rather than through, means w=
e sometimes stray tens of metres off "the line".  This also means we coul=
d be missing animals on the actual line.  I know it would be ideal to wal=
k on "the line" at all times, but it is reality that we don't.)

Linda

messages.subject: Re: Distance from "the line",
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linda:

The perpendicular distance used for your analysis is the distance from
the object to the *line*.  This means that you know where the line is
located during your surveying.

It is not necessary for you to stay on the transect line during your
survey.  Have a look at Figure 3 in "Field trials of line transect
methods applied to estimation of desert tortoise abundance" Anderson et
al. J. Wildlife Mgmt 65:583-597 in 2001.  If you have access to Jstor
(http://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3803111)

The figure shows a search pattern in which one of the observers weaves
on either side of the transect line while another stays on the line.
Perfectly acceptable.  What is not acceptable is missing animals
directly on the line.

messages.subject: Re: Distance from "the line",
messages.body_plain:
Linda, adding to Eric's response, take a look at the duck nest example in c=
hapter 8 of the 2001 distance sampling book.  In particular, look at sectio=
n 8.4.3, where it states '... the observer could go around clumps of such v=
egetation ... the measurements must be taken from the transect centreline, =
not to the observer who may be away from the centreline.'  This is because =
object density may vary with thickness of vegetation, and if the line meand=
ers to avoid the thicker vegetation, you will get biased estimates.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Left truncate or group
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,
I am now having to use Distance to analyse migratory bird data collected =
from point transects in West Africa. My only experience of Distance so fa=
r has been working with some of the exercises in the 2001 distance book a=
nd during the introductory workshop in 2011.

Now that I have real data which I have collected myself, I am facing some=
 challenges with having to make decisions on the most appropriate way to =
analyse my data.

Histograms of the detection distance distributions indicate that I have v=
ery little detection at and close to the points. And although I have quit=
e a few of them along tracks  or at points that I suspect will generally =
have fewer birds, I also strongly suspect that some of these birds have m=
oved away from the point most likely as I was arriving. I suspect also th=
at these birds haven=E2=80=99t returned after the 2 mins settling time th=
at I allowed. I am working with 4 separate migrant species and with two o=
f them, the closest detection distances are as far as 15-25 meters from t=
he point transect where I decided on a radius of 50 m in the field. There=
 also appears to be a certain distance (30-35) where most of my detection=
s occur for most of these species.=20
I am currently considering the two options of either left-truncating this=
 data or grouping it such that my first cut-point includes the groups of =
nearest distances to the point. However, I am concerned that left truncat=
ing or even grouping data collected over what I suspect is now a small wi=
dth may be problematic. Moreover, as using both of these methods will inc=
lude having two separate data sets, I wonder if there is some other way o=
f determining the most appropriate method of the two if I can=E2=80=99t c=
ompare AICs from separate data sets.=20

Can someone suggest a better approach besides these two? And if not, whic=
h of these approaches is best for my situation and is there a way to tell=
 which of these options gives the most reliable estimates, being that I c=
an=E2=80=99t compare the AICs and I don=E2=80=99t have a true =E2=80=98de=
nsity=E2=80=99 with which to compare my estimates as is the case with the=
 other examples in the book.

A second question concerns appropriate model selection. I see that Distan=
ce has the option and the ability to select up to 5 detection function mo=
dels with different keys and series expansions for an analysis where the =
best fit model is selected at the end of it. Is it always best to make us=
e of this option to specify multiple and let it choose the best?

Many thanks for taking time to read this and in anticipation of your help=
ful comments and insights regarding my concerns to help me proceed more c=
onfidently with analysis. Please you can send reply to me at: sti2@st-and=
rews.ac.uk <http://rews.ac.uk>

Sam
